title: Customer proof points + benchmark snippets (sales demo narration) — working doc
content:
Purpose
- Single source of “demo-safe” proof points for AEs/SEs.
- Includes: (a) proof points you can say out loud, (b) benchmark snippets you can show (or not), (c) guardrails on what’s safe to share externally.

How to use (quick)
- 30-min demo: pick 3 proof points max + 1 benchmark visual.
- Default order: Reliability + Production economics + Unified deployment story.
- If asked for numbers: use the “External-safe ranges” below; do NOT freestyle exact figures.

IMPORTANT GUARDRAILS (read before using)
- Demo tenant metrics are SYNTHETIC. Never claim they are from a customer.
- Any customer name/logo requires an approved reference + signed permission. This doc intentionally uses anonymized examples.
- Competitive claims must be framed as “in our tests / typical workloads / depends on model + hardware + prompt shape.”
- When in doubt: use qualitative proof points (predictability, controls, observability) and defer numbers to a follow-up email with PMM review.


SECTION A — External-safe proof points (say out loud)

A1) Production economics (cost + latency control)
- “Redwood is optimized for serving economics, not just ‘can it run.’ You can trade off latency vs unit cost with explicit levers: batching, caching, quantization profiles, and routing.”
- “We show token-level cost + latency breakdowns so you can identify where the spend is actually coming from (prefill vs decode, cache hit rate, long-tail latency).”
- “Most teams don’t need to rebuild their app to optimize—these knobs are on the serving layer with consistent APIs across hosted/dedicated/private.”

Safe add-on line (external):
- “It’s common to see double-digit % cost improvements on steady workloads once batching + caching are tuned.”

Do NOT say externally:
- Exact % savings without context or written follow-up.
- “Guaranteed” savings.

A2) Reliability + graceful degradation
- “The runtime is built for production reliability: you can pin a model version for stability and still configure safe fallback to compatible variants/regions when capacity is constrained.”
- “You can run canaries/A-B and roll back quickly if quality or latency regresses—this is serving-focused lifecycle management.”
- “If something degrades, we want you to degrade gracefully (fallback policy) instead of going hard-down.”

Safe add-on line (external):
- “Teams often care less about peak throughput and more about predictable p95 and predictable failure modes—our platform is designed for that.”

A3) Unified inference across environments
- “Hosted for speed, Dedicated for predictable throughput + isolation, Private for regulated networking—same interface and operational tooling.”
- “You can keep your application integration stable while changing the deployment mode behind the scenes.”

A4) Observability that maps to LLM problems
- “LLM inference isn’t a black box: we break down latency and cost by tokens and give you route/model dashboards, traces, and error analysis.”
- “We provide an operator view for rollouts and fallbacks, not just a raw metrics dump.”

A5) Developer-first onboarding
- “Developers can start with a simple API/SDK and add production controls as they scale—rate limits, quotas, rollouts, routing.”


SECTION B — Benchmark snippets (what to show vs what to keep internal)

B0) Default stance
- Show visuals that are ABOUT behaviors (shapes/trends) more than absolute numbers.
- If you show numbers, show ranges and label them clearly as “example workload.”

B1) Latency terms to use consistently (demo narration)
- TTFT (time to first token): “how fast does streaming start?”
- Decode rate (tokens/sec): “how fast do we generate once we start?”
- p95/p99 latency: “tail matters in production.”

B2) External-safe “ranges” (ONLY if asked; keep it general)
- “In typical chat-style workloads, we aim for low-second TTFT and stable p95 under steady load, with cost controls via batching/caching.”
- “Throughput depends heavily on model size, context length, and output length; Redwood’s runtime focuses on keeping utilization high without blowing up tail latency.”

B3) Internal-only benchmark snippets (for enablement/training; do not paste into external decks)
NOTE: These are useful for coaching the demo story and for internal confidence, but not approved to send externally without PMM + legal review.
- Example (internal training): “With continuous batching + KV/prefix caching enabled on steady workloads, we’ve observed material unit-cost improvements while holding p95 roughly flat.”
- Example (internal training): “Pinned model routes reduce demo regressions; fallback policy reduces hard failures during transient capacity constraints.”


SECTION C — Anonymized customer-style proof points (safe format)

Use these as STORIES (no names), especially if the prospect asks “who else is doing this?”

C1) Payments / fintech platform team (anonymized)
- Problem: “We can’t have unpredictable latency spikes or noisy neighbor behavior during peak hours.”
- What resonated: Dedicated capacity controls + quotas + predictable throughput + clear rollback/fallback story.
- Outcome statement (external-safe): “They wanted predictable performance and clearer operational controls than a generic endpoint.”

C2) Regulated healthcare / security reviewer (anonymized)
- Problem: “We need private networking, audit logs, and clear retention/residency answers.”
- What resonated: Private/VPC deployment option, SSO/SAML + RBAC, audit logs, KMS/HSM integration story.
- Outcome statement (external-safe): “They cared more about governance and auditability than raw benchmark wins.”

C3) Retail search relevance team (anonymized)
- Problem: “Cost sensitivity on embeddings + rerank; need to debug ‘why did relevance change?’”
- What resonated: Cost breakdowns + caching + observability to catch regressions; eval/prompt set story.
- Outcome statement (external-safe): “Console visibility into spend + performance helped them justify rollout decisions.”


SECTION D — Competitive-safe framing (talk track-ready)

D1) Versus ‘just use a cloud endpoint’
- “Cloud endpoints are great for first experiments. We’re built for predictable serving: explicit cost/latency controls, better operator experience, and consistent deployment modes.”
- “We focus on the production surface area: rollouts, fallbacks, token-level analytics, and repeatable economics.”

D2) Versus LLM API aggregators
- “We don’t just provide model access—we provide serving reliability, observability, and cost controls as first-class features.”
- “If you need a stable runtime across hosted/dedicated/private with pinned versions and consistent tooling, that’s our wedge.”

D3) Versus ‘we’ll build our own’
- “You can build a serving stack, but the hidden work is keeping it stable across model/hardware changes while maintaining SLOs and unit economics.”
- “Our goal is to give you control without inheriting the operational tax.”


SECTION E — “Safe to share?” matrix (quick reference)

GREEN (generally safe to say/show)
- Qualitative claims about: deployment flexibility, pinned versions, fallback routing concept, observability views, rollouts, least-privilege keys.
- Screenshots of Console using SYNTHETIC demo tenant (no real org names, no email addresses, no tokens/keys visible).
- Ranges with clear caveats (“depends on model/context length/output length”).

YELLOW (say with caution; prefer follow-up)
- Any numeric benchmark (latency/tokens-sec/$ per 1M tokens). Use ranges and label the workload.
- Any comparison that implies superiority over a named competitor.
- Claims about “cost reduction %” without stating conditions.

RED (do not share in live demo unless explicitly approved)
- Customer names, logos, or identifiable customer architecture.
- Exact internal performance dashboards, capacity utilization charts, or unreleased roadmap items.
- Anything that reveals internal model catalog changes/rollout incidents.


SECTION F — Approved demo-friendly “numbers” (PLACEHOLDER / needs final approval)
Status: NOT FINAL. Do not use externally until Soojin/Camila mark as approved.
- TODO: Decide if we want a single ‘illustrative’ chart (synthetic) showing (a) cost vs batching on/off and (b) p95 impact.
- TODO: Confirm which workloads we’re comfortable standardizing: chat (short + long context), extraction/structured output, embeddings+rereank.

Owner notes / open questions
- Should we standardize phrasing: “Optimize” vs “cost/performance toolkit”? (field feedback says Optimize name confuses some prospects)
- Need a single slide-ready disclaimer sentence for any chart: “Results vary by model, hardware, and prompt; shown for example workload.”
- Need explicit Security sign-off language for showing audit logs in demo (what fields must be redacted?)

Update cadence
- PMM refresh monthly or when model catalog changes impact the demo story.
- If you see reps using ad-hoc numbers: please ping #marketing + link the call snippet (we’ll fix the doc).
